subject: Visual Art
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is practical. Section A is Drawing (from objects, nature or life; 3 hours, 100 marks). Section B is 2-D Creative Design (graphic design, textile design or picture making; 3 hours). Section C is 3-D Creative Design: a project carried out over six months, whose notes and working drawings count for 10%. May/June candidates take A and either B or C; November/December candidates take A and B.

practicals.title: Still-life drawing of a group of man-made objects
practicals.aim: To draw a group of arranged man-made objects as one composition, with accurate proportion, form and tonal value.
materials: Half-imperial cartridge paper (about 38 cm x 56 cm)
Objects such as a bottle, an old radio, a bicycle chain, an enamel pot and a cloth drape
safety: Fix charcoal work with spray fixative only in the open air.
Sit upright, with the board at a comfortable angle.
procedure: Study the group through the viewfinder. Choose landscape or portrait format and place the group so it fills about two-thirds of the paper.
Block in the overall shape lightly, then each object, with simple geometric construction lines (cylinders, boxes, ellipses).
Check proportions by sight-size measuring: hold the pencil at arm's length, measure one object, and compare the others with it.
Correct the ellipses so they get rounder the further they are below or above eye level, and check that the overlaps are correct.
Find the light source. Lay in the mid-tones, then the darks and the cast shadows. Keep the highlights white.
Render textures (shiny metal, glass, cloth) and strengthen the edges. Lightly erase the construction lines that are no longer needed.
practicals.expectedObservations: A good drawing shows correct proportions and overlaps, consistent light and shadow, and convincing textures, with the group set firmly on the surface.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Proportion check: a bottle 30 cm tall and 10 cm wide has a ratio of 3:1. If it is drawn 21 cm tall, it must be 21 / 3 = 7 cm wide. Placement: on paper 56 cm tall, leaving 4 cm top and bottom margins gives a drawing area 48 cm high.
precautions: Keep your arm straight when measuring.
Do not press hard in the early stages.
sourcesOfError: Moving your head changes the view.
commonMistakes: Drawing objects too small in the middle of the paper.
Flat ellipses at the base of cylinders.
examTips: Marks usually reward composition, accurate drawing and proportion, tonal value and rendering, and the overall finish. Use the full three hours.
Put your index number on the back, not on the face of the work.

practicals.title: Nature study: drawing plants, shells and natural forms
practicals.aim: To study a natural object closely and draw it so that its form, structure and pattern of growth come through.
materials: A branch with leaves and a fruit, a snail shell, a fish, a bone or a vegetable such as a garden egg or a bitter-leaf stem
safety: Wash your hands after handling fish, bones or plants.
Do not taste unknown plants.
procedure: Look at the object from several viewpoints and choose the angle that shows the most character.
Lightly draw the main growth lines (stem direction, spiral of the shell, midrib and veins).
Build the shapes on these lines. Measure one part and compare the others with it.
Study details under the hand lens (vein pattern, scales, texture) and draw a magnified detail beside the main drawing.
Add tone or colour to model the form and show the surface.
practicals.expectedObservations: Natural forms follow growth patterns: spirals in shells, branching in stems, and radiating veins. Showing these patterns makes the drawing convincing.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A detail drawn at x3: a leaf 6 cm long is drawn 6 x 3 = 18 cm. A scale bar of 1 cm on the object is drawn 3 cm long.
precautions: Keep the object in the same position throughout.
sourcesOfError: Leaves wilting and changing shape over time.
commonMistakes: Drawing symbols ("leaf shapes") instead of what is actually seen.
examTips: Bring out the beauty of the form and the nature of growth, as the syllabus asks.
Fill the paper with a confident composition.

practicals.title: Life drawing: a posed figure
practicals.aim: To draw a living model in a set pose with correct proportions, balance, structure and form.
apparatus: Plumb line (a string with a weight) or a pencil held vertical
materials: A model (a classmate) posed, for example seated on a stool with one hand on the knee
safety: Let the model rest every 20 to 25 minutes.
Respect the model's dignity and keep them suitably dressed.
procedure: Mark the top and bottom of the figure on the paper so it fills the height.
Use the head length as the unit and mark the head positions down the figure.
Draw the line of action and the centre-of-gravity line (with a plumb line through the pit of the neck to the supporting foot).
Block in the torso, pelvis and limbs as simple forms. Check the angles of the shoulders and hips, which tilt opposite ways when the weight is on one leg.
Refine the contours, hands, feet and clothing folds, and add tone for the form.
practicals.expectedObservations: An adult standing figure is about 7 to 8 heads tall. A seated figure is about 5 to 5.5 heads. The figure looks balanced when the weight line falls through the supporting foot or the seat.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: With 7.5 heads to the figure, a model 168 cm tall has a head of 168 / 7.5 = 22.4 cm. A standing figure drawn 45 cm tall needs a head of 45 / 7.5 = 6 cm.
precautions: Mark the model's position with chalk so the pose can be resumed after breaks.
commonMistakes: A head that is too big.
Hands and feet that are too small.
A figure that floats with no ground or chair.
examTips: Show structure (the skeleton under the clothes) and the pose described in the question exactly.
Include the stool or chair in correct perspective.

practicals.title: One- and two-point perspective drawing
practicals.aim: To draw a street or a classroom corridor in parallel (one-point) perspective and a block of buildings in angular (two-point) perspective.
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Draw the horizon (eye level) line across the paper.
One-point: mark a single vanishing point (VP) on the horizon and draw the walls, windows and road edges to it. Space the receding posts closer and closer together.
Two-point: mark two VPs far apart on the horizon. Draw the nearest vertical corner, then join its top and bottom to both VPs.
Add the verticals for the other corners, doors and windows, all receding to the correct VP.
Use aerial perspective: make distant parts paler, cooler and less detailed.
Add tone and erase the unnecessary construction lines.
practicals.expectedObservations: Parallel lines going away from the viewer meet at the VP. Equal objects look smaller with distance. Lines above eye level slope down to the VP and lines below slope up.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Apparent size is roughly inversely proportional to distance. A 2 m post 5 m away looks twice as tall as the same post 10 m away (5 / 10 = 1/2). If the near post is drawn 8 cm tall, the far post is drawn 4 cm tall.
precautions: Keep the VPs on the horizon.
Place the VPs well apart in two-point perspective so the drawing is not distorted.
Use sharp pencils for construction lines.
commonMistakes: Vertical lines that are not vertical.
examTips: Know the types: aerial, linear (parallel or angular) and foreshortening.
A correct eye level makes objects sit convincingly.

practicals.title: Tonal scale and colour wheel
practicals.aim: To make a 9-step tonal scale and a 12-hue colour wheel, then use them to model a sphere.
materials: Poster colours (red, yellow, blue, white, black)
safety: Do not put brushes in your mouth.
Wash your hands after using paint.
procedure: Rule a strip 18 cm long divided into 9 boxes of 2 cm. Shade them from white (1) to the darkest black (9) in even steps.
Draw a circle and divide it into 12 sectors of 30 degrees.
Paint the primaries (red, yellow, blue) 120 degrees apart, then the secondaries between them, then the tertiaries.
Make tints (adding white) and shades (adding black) of one hue.
Draw a sphere and model it with the tonal scale: highlight, light, half-tone, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow.
practicals.expectedObservations: Complementary colours sit opposite each other and intensify each other when placed side by side. Even tonal steps make the form look round.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Tonal scale: 18 cm / 9 steps = 2 cm per box. Colour wheel: 360 / 12 = 30 degrees per hue. Primaries are 120 degrees apart. Complementary colours are 180 degrees apart.
precautions: Mix enough paint for each area.
commonMistakes: Jumping from pale to dark in one step.
Mixing black into yellow and expecting a clean shade (it turns greenish).
examTips: Define the elements of art (line, colour, shape, form, space, texture) with examples.
Know hue, tint, shade, tone, intensity and value.

practicals.title: Design composition applying the principles of art
practicals.aim: To design two abstract compositions, one with symmetrical and one with asymmetrical balance, showing rhythm, emphasis, harmony and proportion.
safety: Use the compass point carefully.
procedure: Rule two frames 30 cm wide.
Divide one frame by the golden ratio to place a focal point (emphasis).
Build the shapes so they repeat with variation (rhythm). Keep a limited, harmonious colour scheme with one contrasting accent.
Make the second composition symmetrical about a centre line.
Write a short note naming the principles used and where they appear.
practicals.expectedObservations: A focal point placed on the golden section or thirds lines feels more dynamic than one in the dead centre. Repetition gives unity, and variety keeps interest.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Golden ratio division of 30 cm: 30 / 1.618 = 18.54 cm from one side, leaving 11.46 cm. A rule-of-thirds division of the same width gives lines at 10 cm and 20 cm.
commonMistakes: Too many unrelated shapes, which lose unity.
Placing the focal point in the exact centre without reason.
examTips: Name each principle you used and show where it is in the composition.

practicals.title: Preparing tools and materials: stretching paper and caring for brushes
practicals.topic: Art and craft tools and materials
practicals.aim: To stretch watercolour paper on a board, and to clean, store and care for brushes, palettes and drawing tools.
materials: Cartridge or watercolour paper (56 cm x 38 cm)
safety: Cut with the knife against a steel ruler and keep your fingers behind the blade.
procedure: Cut four strips of gummed tape, each about 5 cm longer than the paper edge it goes on.
Wet the paper evenly on both sides with the sponge and let it relax for 2 minutes.
Lay it flat on the board and smooth it from the centre outwards.
Moisten the tape and stick it so that half overlaps the paper and half sits on the board. Let it dry flat.
After painting, wash brushes in water and mild soap, reshape the tips, and dry them standing bristles up.
Clean the palettes, sharpen the pencils with a knife, and store the materials in labelled containers.
practicals.expectedObservations: Stretched paper dries drum-tight and stays flat when wet washes are applied. Unstretched paper cockles.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Tape for paper 56 cm x 38 cm: 2 x (56 + 38) = 188 cm, plus 4 x 5 cm overlap = 208 cm, about 2.1 m.
precautions: Dry the board flat, away from direct heat.
commonMistakes: Leaving brushes standing in water, which bends the bristles.
Using masking tape, which does not hold wet paper.
examTips: Know the materials and how to care for them: brushes (sable, hog, nylon), pencils (H and B grades), papers and palettes.

checkQuestions.explanation: Drying bristles up keeps them in shape.

practicals.title: Formal lettering and notice layout
practicals.aim: To set out and render a brief notice in formal Roman capitals, with correct spacing and layout.
apparatus: Ruling pen or a fine brush
safety: Handle the ruling pen and ink carefully, and cap the ink.
procedure: Read the text and choose the hierarchy: main heading, subheading and details.
Rule the guide lines for the letter heights (for example 6 cm for the heading) and draw margins.
Sketch the letters lightly. Estimate the total length and centre it within the margins.
Adjust the spacing optically. Round letters (O, C, G) and open letters (L, A, T) need less space beside them than straight-sided letters (H, I).
Ink or paint the letters with clean, even strokes and serifs.
Erase the guide lines and check the alignment.
practicals.expectedObservations: Optically spaced lettering looks even. Mechanically equal gaps make round letters look too far apart.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: "SPORTS DAY" on a 50 cm wide board with 4 cm margins on each side: usable width = 42 cm. 9 letters x 3.5 cm = 31.5 cm, plus 7 inter-letter gaps x 0.5 cm = 3.5 cm, plus one word space of 3 cm = 38 cm. Spare = 42 - 38 = 4 cm, so add 2 cm on each side to centre the line.
precautions: Let the ink dry before erasing.
commonMistakes: Running out of space at the end of the line.
examTips: The layout, accuracy of the letterforms and spacing, and neatness carry the marks.
Keep to the wording exactly as given, with correct spelling.

practicals.title: Pictorial poster design
practicals.aim: To design a pictorial poster that combines an illustration with suitable lettering for a public message, for example an anti-cultism or malaria campaign.
materials: Cartridge paper or card (for example 38 cm x 56 cm)
safety: Wash your hands after painting.
procedure: Make thumbnails: try at least three layouts with different emphasis.
Choose a strong single image and a short, bold slogan. Limit the colours to three or four contrasting ones.
Rule the margins and lettering guides. Sketch the illustration and the lettering at full size.
Paint the flat background areas, then the image, then the lettering. Keep the edges clean.
Check that the message can be read from about 3 m away.
practicals.expectedObservations: A strong contrast between the lettering and the background helps legibility. A simple image communicates faster than a crowded one.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Legibility rule of thumb: about 2.5 cm of letter height for each 3 m of viewing distance. A poster read from 6 m needs headline letters of at least 2.5 x 2 = 5 cm.
precautions: Check the spelling before you paint.
sourcesOfError: Paint streaking when it is too thin.
examTips: Examiners look for originality, a clear message, layout, lettering and colour, and finish.

practicals.title: Illustrating a story page
practicals.aim: To illustrate a scene from a given story to fit a set page size and text area.
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Read the passage and choose the moment that best tells the story.
Plan the page: margins, the text block and the image area.
Sketch figures, setting and expressions that match the text (period, costume, mood).
Draw the artwork larger than the print size (for example 150%) for detail. Keep the same proportions.
Ink and colour the artwork, then add a caption or quote from the text.
practicals.expectedObservations: An illustration that agrees with the text in details (clothing, setting, number of characters) supports the story.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A5 page 148 mm x 210 mm with 15 mm margins all round gives an image area of 148 - 30 = 118 mm by 210 - 30 = 180 mm. Drawn at 150%, the artwork is 177 mm x 270 mm. It keeps the same ratio because 177 / 118 = 270 / 180 = 1.5.
precautions: Keep the proportions when you enlarge.
Keep the margins clear of artwork.
sourcesOfError: The proportion changes when the artwork is resized carelessly.
examTips: Show clear storytelling, good figure drawing and suitable style.

practicals.title: Linocut relief print edition
practicals.aim: To design, cut and print a one-colour linocut, and present a numbered edition.
safety: Always cut away from your body and keep the hand that holds the block behind the cutter, using the bench hook.
Warm hard lino slightly (in the sun) to make cutting easier.
procedure: Design the image in strong black-and-white shapes. Any lettering must be reversed on the block.
Transfer the design to the lino and fill in the areas that will print, so it is clear what to cut.
Cut away the non-printing areas: V-gouge for lines and U-gouge for clearing. Make a proof print and adjust.
Roll ink thinly on the slab until it hisses, then ink the block evenly.
Lay the paper on the block against registration marks and rub it all over with the baren.
Pull the print, dry it, and repeat. Sign each print in pencil with the edition number (for example 3/10), the title and your name.
practicals.expectedObservations: The raised (uncut) areas print and the cut areas stay white. The image prints as a mirror image of the block.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Centring a 20 cm x 25 cm block on 30 cm x 40 cm paper: side margins = (30 - 20) / 2 = 5 cm each. The vertical spare is 40 - 25 = 15 cm, placed as 6 cm at the top and 9 cm at the bottom (a weighted bottom margin).
precautions: Register each sheet the same way.
Clean the block and roller after printing.
sourcesOfError: Ink too thick, which fills the fine lines.
examTips: Explain relief printing: the raised surface prints.
Present a clean, consistent edition with correct numbering.

practicals.title: Stencil and screen printing
practicals.aim: To print a two-colour design onto paper or fabric using cut stencils and a silk screen.
safety: Cut on a mat and keep your fingers behind the blade.
Use solvents in a ventilated area.
procedure: Separate the design into colour layers and cut one stencil per colour, with registration marks.
Tape stencil 1 under the screen and set up the registration (hinges, or corner marks on the base).
Pull ink across with the squeegee at 45 degrees and even pressure, for one or two passes.
Print all the copies in colour 1 and let them dry.
Clean the screen, fit stencil 2, align it with the marks, and print colour 2.
Discard the misprints and number the good prints.
practicals.expectedObservations: Accurate registration lines the colours up. Ink only passes where the stencil is open.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: To get 20 good prints with about 10% spoilage, print 20 x 1.1 = 22 copies in the first colour.
precautions: Keep the screen clean so the mesh does not clog.
commonMistakes: Islands (such as the middle of an O) falling out of the stencil because no bridges were left.
examTips: Explain registration and how to plan stencils with bridges.

practicals.title: Package design: a cereal box net
practicals.aim: To construct the net of a cereal box and design its graphics (brand name, logo, illustration and information panel).
safety: Cut against a steel ruler and keep your fingers clear of the blade.
procedure: Decide the box size: 20 cm wide x 7 cm deep x 30 cm tall.
Draw the net: four side panels in a row (20, 7, 20 and 7 cm), a 1.5 cm glue flap, and top and bottom flaps 7 cm deep.
Design the front (brand name, product image, key claim), the back (story or activity), the sides (nutrition facts, net weight, NAFDAC number placeholder) and the top.
Paint or colour the artwork on the flat net.
Score the fold lines, cut out, fold, and glue.
practicals.expectedObservations: An accurate net folds into a square, closed box. Graphics continue correctly across the folds only if they were planned on the net.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Net width = 2 x (20 + 7) + 1.5 = 55.5 cm. Net height = 30 + 2 x 7 = 44 cm. A sheet of at least 56 cm x 44 cm is needed.
precautions: Check that the artwork is the right way up on each panel.
sourcesOfError: Card thickness affects the fold allowance.
examTips: Show the net with dimensions and a 3-D view of the finished box.
Include the product information that real packages carry.

practicals.title: Designing a logo and invitation card in a graphics package
practicals.aim: To design a school club logo and an invitation card using vector software (for example CorelDRAW or Inkscape) and export them for print.
apparatus: Computer with CorelDRAW, Inkscape or a similar program
safety: Sit upright with the screen at eye level.
Take short screen breaks.
procedure: Sketch the ideas on paper first.
Create a new document of the right size (for example A5 for the invitation, 10 cm x 10 cm for the logo).
Draw shapes with the rectangle, ellipse and Bezier tools. Combine and weld them, then fill and outline.
Add text, choose suitable fonts, and convert the text to curves for the final logo.
Arrange the invitation layout with alignment guides and place the logo.
Save the native file, then export as PDF or PNG at 300 dpi for printing.
practicals.expectedObservations: Vector shapes stay sharp at any size. Raster images exported at low resolution look pixelated when printed.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Pixels = size in inches x dpi. A 10 cm logo at 300 dpi: 10 / 2.54 x 300 = 1,181 pixels wide. An A4 page (210 mm x 297 mm) at 300 dpi is about 2,480 x 3,508 pixels.
precautions: Use CMYK colours for print and check the fonts.
sourcesOfError: Screen colours differ from printed colours.
commonMistakes: Leaving text as editable fonts that are missing on the printing computer.
examTips: Name the tools you used (pick, shape, text, fill, weld) and describe the steps.

practicals.title: Textile design: a two-metre tie-dye or batik length
practicals.aim: To design and dye a 2 m length of unsewn cotton in a planned pattern, by tie-dye or batik.
materials: 2 m of scoured white cotton (about 300 g)
Salt and soda ash (for reactive dye)
safety: Handle dye powders and alkalis with gloves and a mask, and avoid inhaling them.
Never heat wax over an open flame without a water bath.
Ventilate the room.
procedure: Plan the full-length design on paper at a scale of 1:10, showing the repeat.
Mark the fabric lightly with chalk.
Apply the resist: tie (circles, pleats, folding) or wax.
Prepare the dye bath and dye the fabric for the time given in the recipe, stirring gently.
Rinse until the water runs clear. Remove the ties or wax, wash, dry and iron.
Present the length neatly folded or hung, with your design sheet.
practicals.expectedObservations: Resisted areas stay pale. A planned repeat gives an even, professional pattern over the whole length.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For 300 g of fabric at a 1:20 liquor ratio: water = 6 L. Dye at 2% = 6 g. With a recipe of 50 g/L salt and 10 g/L soda ash: salt = 300 g and soda ash = 60 g. Design at 1:10: the 200 cm length is drawn as 20 cm.
sourcesOfError: Hard water or a wrong temperature affects the shade.
commonMistakes: A length shorter than the 2 m minimum.
Patchy dyeing from overcrowding the bucket.
examTips: The syllabus requires a piece at least 2 m long. Check the length before you start.
Neatness of pattern and colour harmony carry marks.

practicals.title: Appliqué cushion cover
practicals.aim: To design and make an appliqué panel for a cushion cover, with shaped fabric pieces sewn onto a foundation.
safety: Keep pins in a cushion, not your mouth.
Switch the iron off after use.
procedure: Design the motif on paper at full size (40 cm x 40 cm).
Make templates for each shape and cut them from fabric, adding turnings.
Arrange the pieces on the foundation, then pin and tack them.
Stitch the edges with slip stitch, blanket stitch or machine satin stitch.
Make up the cushion: cut the back, join with seams, and insert a zip or an envelope opening.
Press and finish.
practicals.expectedObservations: Contrasting colours make the motif stand out. Neat, even edge stitches prevent fraying.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For a finished cover of 40 cm x 40 cm with 1.5 cm seam allowance on each side, cut the foundation 40 + 2 x 1.5 = 43 cm square.
examTips: Show the design, the colour scheme and the stitches in your notes.

practicals.title: Tapestry wall hanging
practicals.aim: To weave a small pictorial tapestry on a frame loom from a cartoon (full-size design).
materials: Wool, cotton or raffia wefts in several colours
safety: Smooth the frame so there are no splinters.
procedure: Draw the cartoon at full size (30 cm x 40 cm) and place it behind the warp.
Warp the loom at 5 ends per cm.
Weave a plain heading.
Build up the colour areas with separate weft butterflies, using slit, dovetail or interlock joins.
Beat each pick so the weft completely covers the warp (weft-faced).
Finish with a heading, knot the warp ends, and mount the hanging on a dowel.
practicals.expectedObservations: A weft-faced tapestry hides the warp. Bubbled picks prevent the sides from narrowing.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Ends = 30 cm x 5 = 150. With each end 40 cm plus 20 cm for knotting and loom waste (60 cm), the warp needs 150 x 0.6 = 90 m.
examTips: Name the joins (slit, dovetail, interlock) and explain why tapestry is weft-faced.

practicals.title: Picture making: painting a scene from everyday life
practicals.aim: To create an illustrative composition in paint on a given theme (for example "Market day" or "Fetching water"), enlarged from a sketch with a grid.
materials: Cartridge paper or card (50 cm x 40 cm)
safety: Wash your hands after using paint.
Do not eat while painting.
procedure: Interpret the theme. Make thumbnail sketches of figures, setting and the focal point.
Draw a 10 cm x 8 cm composition sketch with a grid of 2 cm squares (5 x 4 squares).
Draw the same 5 x 4 grid on the 50 cm x 40 cm paper (10 cm squares) and transfer the drawing square by square.
Block in the large colour areas: background first, then the middle ground and foreground.
Model the forms with light and shade, and add details and textures.
Check the overall harmony, strengthen the focal point, and finish the edges.
practicals.expectedObservations: Gridding keeps the proportions when enlarging. Warm, intense colours come forward and cool, greyed colours recede.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Enlarging a 10 cm x 8 cm sketch to 50 cm x 40 cm is a scale factor of 50 / 10 = 5 (and 40 / 8 = 5). The 2 cm grid squares become 10 cm squares, and the area grows 5 x 5 = 25 times.
precautions: Keep the grid squares the same ratio as the sketch.
sourcesOfError: The grid ratio does not match the format.
examTips: Marks go to interpretation of the theme, composition, drawing, colour and technique, and finish.
Finish within the time, because an unfinished work loses marks.

practicals.title: Photography: exposure and a photogram
practicals.aim: To shoot a portrait and a landscape with correct exposure, and to make a photogram using objects on light-sensitive paper.
apparatus: Camera or smartphone with manual mode
Darkroom with safelight or a light-tight box
materials: Objects such as leaves, keys and lace
safety: Darkroom chemicals irritate the skin, so use tongs and gloves and keep the room ventilated.
Never mix chemicals.
Do not eat in the darkroom.
procedure: Shoot a portrait with soft side light and the background slightly out of focus. Shoot a landscape using the rule of thirds.
Record the shutter speed and aperture for each, and compare equivalent settings.
Photogram: under the safelight, place objects on the photographic paper. Make a test strip by exposing it to the lamp for 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 seconds.
Develop the test strip (developer about 1 min, stop bath, fixer), choose the best time, then expose the final print.
Wash and dry the prints, then mount and label them.
practicals.expectedObservations: In a photogram, areas covered by objects stay white and exposed areas turn black. Translucent objects give greys. A longer exposure gives a darker print.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Equivalent exposures: f/8 at 1/125 s lets in the same light as f/5.6 at 1/250 s, because opening one stop doubles the light and halving the time halves it. Test strip: if the 6 s band gives the best black, use 6 s for the final print.
precautions: Keep the paper in the dark until exposure.
commonMistakes: Underexposed or blurred shots (use a tripod).
examTips: Know the exposure triangle (aperture, shutter speed, ISO) and simple photo tricks (photogram, distortion).

practicals.title: Mosaic panel
practicals.aim: To make a mosaic picture from small, regular-shaped coloured pieces fixed onto a board.
materials: Plywood or hardboard (40 cm x 30 cm)
Tesserae (1.5 cm pieces of coloured tile, glass, card or seeds)
safety: Wear goggles and gloves when cutting tiles or glass, because shards fly.
Sweep up the shards carefully.
procedure: Draw the design to size on the board, with clear outlines and colour areas.
Sort the tesserae by colour and cut them to size.
Lay the outlines of the main shapes first (andamento, the flow of the rows), then fill the background, keeping gaps of about 2 mm.
Let the glue set, then grout, wipe off the excess, and polish.
Frame or edge the panel.
practicals.expectedObservations: Following the contours with the rows of tesserae makes the forms clear. Even gaps give a neat, unified surface.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Tile pitch = 1.5 cm piece + 0.2 cm gap = 1.7 cm. Across 40 cm: 40 / 1.7 = 23.5, so 23 pieces. Down 30 cm: 30 / 1.7 = 17.6, so 17 pieces. Total = 23 x 17 = 391 tesserae. With 10% for cutting waste, about 430.
precautions: Do not let the glue skin over before placing the pieces.
commonMistakes: Random placing that ignores the contours.
examTips: Distinguish mosaic (regular pieces) from collage (irregular materials).

practicals.title: Collage composition
practicals.aim: To make a picture by combining irregular-shaped materials (fabric, paper, natural objects) on a surface.
materials: Magazine paper, fabric scraps, sand, seeds, sawdust and dried leaves
safety: Use scissors carefully.
Wash your hands after using glue.
procedure: Sketch a composition on a theme and mark the rule-of-thirds lines for the focal point.
Sort the materials by colour, tone and texture.
Tear or cut the shapes and arrange them without glue to test the composition.
Glue the background first, then the middle ground and the foreground, overlapping for depth.
Press flat under a weight, then trim the edges.
practicals.expectedObservations: Contrasts of texture and tone create interest. Overlapping builds depth.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Rule of thirds on 45 cm x 30 cm: vertical lines at 15 cm and 30 cm, horizontal lines at 10 cm and 20 cm. The focal point goes at one of the four crossings, for example (15 cm, 10 cm).
precautions: Apply glue thinly so the paper does not wrinkle.
sourcesOfError: Organic materials can decay or attract insects unless sealed.
examTips: Name the materials used and explain your choices.

practicals.title: Sculpture: modelling and firing a clay figure
practicals.aim: To model a figure in clay from a maquette, hollow it, dry it and fire it.
safety: Firing is supervised.
Hollowing prevents explosions in the kiln.
Wipe clay dust up damp.
procedure: Make a 15 cm maquette (small model) and a working drawing.
Scale it up to 45 cm using callipers. Build solid over a newspaper core, or coil-build it hollow.
Model the main masses, then the details and the surface texture.
At leather-hard, cut it open, hollow it to an even 1.5 cm wall, rejoin with score and slip, and make a small vent hole.
Dry it slowly under polythene, then fire it.
Patinate or finish it (for example with shoe polish, oxides or paint) and mount it on a base.
practicals.expectedObservations: Even, hollow walls survive firing. Solid, thick lumps crack or explode.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Scaling from a 15 cm maquette to 45 cm: linear factor = 3, so volume (and mass) grows 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 times. A solid 0.4 kg maquette would become 0.4 x 27 = 10.8 kg if solid, which is why the large figure must be hollowed.
precautions: Hollow the work and vent it.
commonMistakes: Leaving metal armature inside clay that will be fired.
examTips: Clay works must be fired. Submit notes, diagrams and working drawings (10% of the 3-D marks).

practicals.title: Product design: a scale model of an industrial product
practicals.aim: To design and build a scale model of a product (for example a car, a phone or a cosmetic bottle) from card, wood or papier-mâché.
materials: Card, balsa or softwood, foam, papier-mâché
safety: Cut away from your body.
Wear a mask when sanding.
Ventilate when painting.
procedure: Research the real product and record its true dimensions.
Choose a scale and draw the orthographic views (front, side, plan) at that scale.
Build the main body from the material (laminated card, a carved foam block, or wood).
Add the details (wheels, buttons, labels) to scale.
Prime, sand, paint and finish. Label the model with its scale.
practicals.expectedObservations: Accurate orthographic drawings lead to a well-proportioned model.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: At 1:10, a car 4.2 m long, 1.8 m wide and 1.5 m high becomes 42 cm x 18 cm x 15 cm.
precautions: Let the paint dry between coats.
sourcesOfError: Material thickness affects the final dimensions.
examTips: Submit the working drawings and notes with the model.

practicals.title: Ceramics: a hand-built or thrown flower vase
practicals.aim: To make and fire a flower vase by coiling, slab building or throwing, sized to allow for shrinkage.
safety: Firing is supervised.
Control dust by cleaning damp.
procedure: Draw the vase with its fired dimensions. Allow for 10% shrinkage.
Make a card profile template.
Build or throw the vase, checking it against the template.
Decorate it at leather-hard (incising, burnishing, slip).
Dry it slowly, bisque fire it, then glaze and glost fire it (or burnish it and leave it unglazed).
practicals.expectedObservations: With the shrinkage allowance, the fired vase meets the target size. Even walls fire safely.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For a fired height of 25 cm with 10% shrinkage, make it 25 / 0.9 = 27.78 cm, about 27.8 cm, when wet.
precautions: Keep the foot free of glaze.
sourcesOfError: Actual shrinkage differs from the estimate.
commonMistakes: Glazed foot sticking to the kiln shelf.
examTips: Clay works must be fired, and notes and working drawings count for 10% of the marks.

practicals.title: Basketry: a coiled table mat
practicals.aim: To design and make a coiled raffia and grass table mat 30 cm in diameter with a coloured pattern.
safety: Store needles safely.
procedure: Plan the colour pattern on a circle drawing.
Start a tight centre and wrap and stitch the coil, keeping the core 1 cm thick with the gauge.
Change raffia colours where the pattern needs it.
Continue for 15 rounds to reach 30 cm.
Taper the core and finish the edge neatly.
Press flat under a weight.
practicals.expectedObservations: An even core and regular stitching give a flat, round mat.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Radius 15 cm with a 1 cm coil = 15 rounds. The mean diameters 1, 3, ... 29 cm add up to 225 cm, so the core length is about pi x 225 = 707 cm (7.07 m).
commonMistakes: Stitches too tight, so the mat cups.
examTips: Basketry works may be made in cane, raffia and similar materials. Show the design and a material estimate in your notes.

practicals.title: Jewellery: a beaded necklace
practicals.aim: To design and construct a necklace from beads, seeds or shells, with a correct length and a secure clasp.
materials: Beads (8 mm) and spacers (2 mm), or local seeds and cowries
safety: Wear goggles when cutting wire.
Keep small beads away from young children.
procedure: Sketch the design with the bead sequence and colour pattern.
Measure the finished length (45 cm) and subtract the clasp length.
Calculate the number of beads and spacers needed.
Thread the beads in the planned sequence on the wire, with a little slack.
Attach the clasp with crimp beads, squeeze them with the pliers, and trim the ends.
Test the strength and the fit.
practicals.expectedObservations: A regular pattern and a well-crimped clasp give a durable, attractive piece.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Beaded length = 45 - 2 (clasp) = 43 cm. Each bead plus spacer = 0.8 + 0.2 = 1.0 cm, so 43 / 1.0 = 43 beads and 43 spacers. Cost: 43 beads x N50 = N2,150, plus clasp and wire N800, total N2,950.
precautions: Count the beads before you finish.
commonMistakes: A wire too tight, so the necklace is stiff.
A loose crimp, so it comes apart.
examTips: Show the design and the material costing in your notes.
Present the necklace on a mount or a stand.

practicals.title: Calabash decoration by incising and pyrography
practicals.aim: To decorate a calabash with an evenly spaced traditional motif by incising, scraping and pyrography (burning).
apparatus: Hot iron rod or pyrography pen
materials: A dried, cleaned calabash (about 30 cm in diameter)
safety: Incise away from your body.
Hot rods cause burns, so use a holder and a safe stand.
Work in a ventilated area.
procedure: Soak, scrape and dry the calabash. Sand the surface smooth.
Measure the circumference and divide it into equal segments with a paper strip.
Draw the motifs lightly in pencil (geometric bands, birds or symbols).
Incise the outlines, scrape the background areas for tonal contrast, and burn the lines or areas with the hot rod.
Rub in dye or polish if wanted, then wipe and seal with oil or varnish.
practicals.expectedObservations: Incised and burnt lines contrast with the smooth skin of the calabash. Even segments give a balanced, rhythmic design.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Circumference of a 30 cm calabash = pi x 30 = 94.25 cm. Twelve motifs need 94.25 / 12 = 7.85 cm each, or 360 / 12 = 30 degrees apart.
precautions: Use shallow cuts so the shell does not split.
sourcesOfError: An irregular calabash shape makes the segments uneven.
examTips: Name the decoration methods (incising, scraping, pyrography, dyeing, beading) and the traditional sources (for example Oyo and Bida calabash carvers).
